docs.x: Judge Judith C. McCarthy, S.D.N.Y.. Conduct at trial (trap): Stand when court opens, the jury enters or exits, and when addressing the court; examine from the lectern; address the court, not opposing counsel; use surnames. One attorney per witness, and the attorney objecting on direct handles cross. State only the legal grounds for objections. docs.x: Judge Robyn F. Tarnofsky, S.D.N.Y.. Pretrial (consent cases): After discovery closes, the court issues a scheduling order for the pretrial conference and Joint Pretrial Order. docs.x: Judge Angel D. Mitchell, D. Kan.. ADR and settlement reports: Plaintiff makes a good-faith settlement proposal and defendant a counter-proposal by set dates. Confidential reports go only to the magistrate judge, never to the district judge or the Clerk’s Office, and must detail settlement efforts (including amounts offered), case evaluation, prospects, and a specific ADR recommendation. If the parties disagree, the party seeking the order files a motion and memorandum with the proposed order attached. The form reminds counsel of Rule 26(g) certification duties and mandatory sanctions (for example, for overbroad requests or boilerplate objections). Depositions follow the court’s written deposition guidelines.

docs.t: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer (D. Kan.) — Motions and page limits
docs.x: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer, D. Kan.. Motions and page limits: Page limits for principal briefs, responses, and replies follow D. Kan. Rule 7.1. The court plans to decide timely, unextended dispositive motions about 60 days before trial. Stipulations on discovery procedures are encouraged, but not for extensions that interfere with the discovery, motion, or trial deadlines.

docs.t: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer (D. Kan.) — Pretrial conference and order (trap)
docs.x: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer, D. Kan.. Pretrial conference and order (trap): Defense counsel emails the proposed pretrial order, in Word and in Judge Birzer’s form, to chambers by the set date; it must not be filed. To appear by phone, email chambers 7 days before the conference; the judge may require in-person attendance if the order is not in the right format. The order must be a single joint document; disagreements go in bracketed notations, and separate orders are unacceptable. Do not title it “Plaintiff’s,” “Defendant’s,” or “Proposed.” Factual contentions should be no more than 1–2 pages per party in simple cases and 4–5 pages in complex cases, yet specific enough for each claim and defense to survive a dispositive motion. Pare down claims and defenses, list abandoned ones, correlate each theory to a count, and state damages claim by claim with computations. The pretrial order supersedes

docs.t: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer (D. Kan.) — Stipulations, trial, and settlement
docs.x: Judge Gwynne E. Birzer, D. Kan.. Stipulations, trial, and settlement: Make stipulated facts and exhibit lists as comprehensive as possible, at least for the summary-judgment record; if not ready to stipulate for trial, propose a separate deadline (for example, 5 days before trial) to confer and file stipulations. The trial setting is not a “special” or “No. 1” setting unless ordered; stay in touch with the trial judge’s courtroom deputy in the month before the docket. Only the trial judge can change it. Under D. Kan. Rule 40.3, notify the court immediately of any settlement; jury costs may be assessed unless the jury coordinator is notified at least one full business day before trial.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — No bench conferences; raise issues early (trap)
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. No bench conferences; raise issues early (trap): The goal is at least six solid hours of uninterrupted testimony every trial day. Absent extraordinary circumstances the judge strongly prefers to avoid repeated bench conferences; anticipate most significant evidentiary issues with a timely motion in limine. Matters outside the jury’s presence should be scheduled for 8:30 a.m., recesses, lunch, or after the trial day, with reasonable advance notice. The court may make counsel move on to other matters or witnesses and rule at the next recess. Disclose witnesses (and preferably all exhibits) expected to be used to opposing counsel by 5:30 p.m. the day before, unless the final pretrial order sets a different deadline.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Witnesses and exhibits
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Witnesses and exhibits: Have enough witnesses present for a full day; no dead time. A witness on the stand at a recess must be back on the stand before the jury returns, and a new witness should wait in the front row ready to be sworn. Pre-admit as many exhibits as possible by stipulation at the limine conference held shortly before trial. Use of the court’s evidence display equipment is encouraged but not required; practice with it before trial. Before using a deposition to impeach, give the judge an extra copy of the transcript.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Jury selection: In civil trials the court ordinarily seats fourteen prospective jurors, each side has three peremptory challenges, and eight jurors deliberate with no alternates. The court conducts most voir dire, with about 30 minutes per side for supplemental questioning, unless the parties agree in advance and the court approves attorney-controlled voir dire. Proposed voir dire questions need not be filed unless a topic is expected to be extremely controversial or sensitive. Do not repeat the court’s questions, argue the case, seek promises beyond deciding on the evidence and instructions, examine jurors on law, instructions, or hypotheticals, or try to ingratiate or indoctrinate.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Openings, closings, and trial hours
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Openings, closings, and trial hours: Openings typically 20 minutes per party; if all counsel agree, the court will consider openings to the full panel. Closings typically 30–45 minutes per party, after the court instructs the jury. Counsel must be present at 8:30 a.m. on the first day to review procedures with the courtroom deputy. Jury hours are 9:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. and 1:15 p.m. to 4:45 p.m. unless notified otherwise. Give the court reporter a business card and a typed list of unusual or technical names and terms.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Objections and examination (trap)
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Objections and examination (trap): Absent agreement or advance permission, only one attorney per party examines or cross-examines a given witness, and the attorney who objects during direct is the one who cross-examines. State only the legal ground for an objection, with no further argument unless the court asks, and do not argue after the ruling.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Courtroom etiquette
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Courtroom etiquette: Stand when court opens, recesses, and adjourns, when the jury enters or leaves, when addressing or being addressed by the court, and for openings and closings. Counsel need not stand at the lectern to examine witnesses and may approach a witness for an obvious reason, such as handing over an exhibit, without asking. Do not perch near the witness box, get within a few feet of the jury box, or make concerted eye contact with jurors outside voir dire, opening, and closing. Use surnames with titles, never first names or nicknames, and avoid disparaging remarks toward opposing counsel.

docs.t: Judge James P. O’Hara (D. Kan.) — Sequestered witnesses
docs.x: Judge James P. O’Hara, D. Kan.. Sequestered witnesses: If witnesses are sequestered under Fed. R. Evid. 615, counsel must ensure each witness understands not to discuss their own or any other witness’s testimony with anyone except counsel, and to notify the court promptly if anyone tries to discuss it.

docs.x: Judge David P. Rush, W.D. Mo.. Criminal pretrial motions (trap): Pretrial motions are due within 20 days from the date of the scheduling and trial order; suggestions in opposition are due 10 days after that. For a defendant represented by counsel, the court accepts pretrial filings only from counsel; pro se filings are not accepted. Motions in limine are due no later than 7 days before trial, with suggestions in opposition within 3 days after the motion is filed; the order says copies should be faxed to opposing counsel and the court once filed. Proposed stipulations go in writing to opposing counsel and the court no later than 14 days before trial.

docs.t: Judge David P. Rush (W.D. Mo.) — Criminal discovery from the government
docs.x: Judge David P. Rush, W.D. Mo.. Criminal discovery from the government: Within 10 days of the order, the government must disclose the defendant’s criminal record and prior felony convictions it will use to impeach, the defendant’s statements and grand jury testimony, and Rule 16 documents, objects, and examination and test reports. Also within 10 days: a list of seized evidence (location, date and time, who seized it, and witnesses, or the reports instead), all electronic surveillance by date with logs, recordings, and transcripts, and every identification procedure (or the reports instead). The parties agree to provide Jencks Act material at least 14 days before trial. The defendant’s reciprocal Rule 16 production follows the government’s compliance.

docs.t: Judge David P. Rush (W.D. Mo.) — Brady, Giglio, and informants
docs.x: Judge David P. Rush, W.D. Mo.. Brady, Giglio, and informants: Brady material is due within 10 days of the order and entrapment information within 14 days of the order. No later than 14 days before trial, the government must disclose Giglio impeachment material, witness promises, agreements, and payments, Rule 404(b) notice, and, unless it claims privilege, informant names, addresses, inducements, prior testimony, psychiatric treatment, narcotic habit, and counsel. An informant who objects to disclosing an address must be produced to defense counsel to see whether the informant will consent to an interview. Information the government will use to prove relevant offense conduct or an upward departure is due within 14 days of trial or a change-of-plea hearing.

docs.x: Judge David P. Rush, W.D. Mo.. A defendant who gives Rule 12.2(b) notice must identify mental-condition experts and summarize their opinions 30 days before trial; the government’s responsive summary is due 10 days before trial. Rule 16 expert summaries: the government’s are due no later than 14 days before trial, and the defendant’s no later than 5 days before trial.

All time calculations follow the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure.

docs.t: Judge Lajuana M. Counts (W.D. Mo.) — Mediation agreement and confidentiality
docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Mediation agreement and confidentiality: By participating, parties agree to the attached Mediation/Settlement Conference Agreement: settlement is voluntary, Judge Counts serves as a neutral mediator who gives no legal advice, and information shared in caucus may be passed on unless the party says not to. docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Criminal scheduling and pretrial conferences (trap): The judge holds monthly scheduling conferences and pretrial conferences for the joint criminal trial docket. Unless you plan to stay on the current trial docket, file a motion to continue; the scheduling conference is still held to review discovery. All parties must appear in person at the pretrial conference unless a continuance has been granted or a change-of-plea hearing has been scheduled; schedule a change of plea with the District Judge’s courtroom deputy. docs.t: Judge Lajuana M. Counts (W.D. Mo.) — Trial schedule and decorum
docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Trial schedule and decorum: Trial typically runs 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, with morning and afternoon breaks; substantive issues are taken up before 9:00 a.m., during breaks, or after 5:00 p.m. when possible. Stand when addressing or addressed by the court, direct remarks to the court rather than opposing counsel, avoid visible reactions to testimony or rulings, and raise jury comfort matters out of the jury’s hearing. Give the courtroom deputy a glossary of technical, medical, or unusual terms before hearings and at the pretrial conference.

docs.t: Judge Lajuana M. Counts (W.D. Mo.) — Witnesses and objections (trap)
docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Witnesses and objections (trap): Address adult witnesses as “Mr.,” “Ms.,” or “Dr.,” never by first name. Direct, cross, redirect, and recross only; anything more needs leave. Ask permission before approaching a witness, and let witnesses finish their answers and explain a yes-or-no answer. Object by saying only “objection” and the legal ground (for example, leading or hearsay); to argue it, approach the bench. Witnesses stay in the witness chair unless the court allows them to step down to reference an exhibit.

docs.t: Judge Lajuana M. Counts (W.D. Mo.) — Exhibits, instructions, and deliberations
docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Exhibits, instructions, and deliberations: Mark each exhibit with a sticker showing the offering party and a number matching the exhibit list given to the courtroom deputy before trial. The court usually rules on evidentiary objections at the pretrial conference and pre-admits as many exhibits as reasonable, but only exhibits actually admitted at trial go to the jury. Closing argument length is set near the end of trial, usually at the instruction conference. Instructions are read before closings; jurors get copies of the instructions but only one verdict form. During deliberations, keep your exhibits assembled in the courtroom and stay near the courthouse, telling the deputy where you will be. Afterward, retrieve exhibits and sign the receipt; do not contact jurors without the court’s permission.

docs.t: Judge Lajuana M. Counts (W.D. Mo.) — Contact and equipment
docs.x: Judge Lajuana M. Counts, W.D. Mo.. Contact and equipment: Kansas City (Whittaker Courthouse), chambers 6672, Courtroom 6E. Chambers 816-512-5775; courtroom deputy Traci Chorny, 816-512-5789. docs.t: Judge W. Brian Gaddy (W.D. Mo.) — Who must attend mediations and settlement conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Who must attend mediations and settlement conferences (trap): Lead trial counsel must personally attend, as must parties with full and complete settlement authority. An entity party sends a representative other than counsel of record who can make the ultimate settlement decision or has enough stature to reach the decision makers directly during all scheduled times. The representative may not be someone simply given a pre-approved amount and, absent compelling circumstances, may not be a material fact witness. If settlement needs an insurer’s approval, an insurer representative with full and complete authority must personally attend.

docs.t: Judge W. Brian Gaddy (W.D. Mo.) — Remote participation (trap)
docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Remote participation (trap): Absent extenuating circumstances, no participant may attend by phone or video instead of in person. A party wanting a remote appearance should first seek opposing counsel’s approval and tell the court of the agreement or disagreement when scheduling with court staff. With all parties’ agreement, the court will strongly consider an advance request; without it, remote appearance is allowed only for extreme hardship or other extenuating circumstances. A request to hold the whole session by videoconference should be made at scheduling, but the court strongly prefers in-person sessions.

docs.t: Judge W. Brian Gaddy (W.D. Mo.) — Settlement statements (trap)
docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Settlement statements (trap): Each party’s statement is due no later than 3 business days before the session, emailed to courtroom deputy Melissa Nolte (Melissa_Nolte@mow.uscourts.gov), not filed on ECF. A late statement cancels the session and may be reported to the MAP Director and/or the presiding judge. Sharing it with opposing counsel is optional. Maximum 5 pages, covering: each attendee’s name and title; a brief case summary; key disputed factual and legal issues; relief sought, estimated damages, and any damage caps; desired non-monetary terms; prior negotiations and when they occurred; any insurer, policy type, and limits; outstanding liens and whether a lienholder representative should attend; whether joint sessions would help; and other issues.

docs.t: Judge W. Brian Gaddy (W.D. Mo.) — Session format and timing
docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Session format and timing: The court strongly encourages exchanging demands and offers before the session if the parties have not discussed settlement. Sessions generally run 9:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m.; if more time is needed, say so when the session is first scheduled. The court may open with all participants to cover logistics and confidentiality and allow brief presentations, then hold private meetings with each side; it may skip the joint session if it would not help.

docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Confidentiality, compliance, and rescheduling: Statements made during the session are confidential, may not be shared with non-participants, and are inadmissible at trial. No part of a videoconference session may be recorded or rebroadcast. Participants must comply with the order and the court’s MAP General Order; noncompliance is reported to the assigned district judge and/or the MAP Director and may draw sanctions. Contact chambers as soon as possible to cancel or reschedule.

docs.t: Judge W. Brian Gaddy (W.D. Mo.) — Arraignment on a superseding indictment
docs.x: Judge W. Brian Gaddy, W.D. Mo.. Arraignment on a superseding indictment: The judge’s waiver form lets a defendant waive personal appearance and enter a plea to all counts, but it does not waive the arraignment itself: counsel for the defendant and the government must appear, in person or by video teleconference. File the signed waiver at least 2 business days before the arraignment so the court can accept or decline it and notify the U.S. Marshals Service about transportation.

The October 23, 2026 memo pairs each pretrial conference with a Joint Accelerated Criminal Jury Trial Docket date (for example, a December 8, 2026 conference for the January 4, 2027 docket).

Motions in limine are due no later than 7 days before trial (the order says to fax copies to opposing counsel and the court), with suggestions in opposition within 3 days after filing. Proposed stipulations go to opposing counsel and the court in writing no later than 7 days before trial.

Jencks Act material is due at least 10 days before trial by agreement. Due before trial: government expert summaries 30 days, defense expert summaries 14 days; Giglio material, government witness and exhibit lists 10 days; witness inducements, informant information (unless privilege is claimed), Rule 404(b) notice, and defense witness and exhibit lists 7 days. docs.t: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. (W.D. Mo.) — Civil motions
docs.x: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr., W.D. Mo.. Civil motions: Dispositive motions need a separate section of individually numbered facts, and opposing suggestions must begin with a concise list of facts claimed to be genuinely disputed; summary judgment motions must comply with Local Rules 7.0 and 56.1. Daubert motions have their own deadline (the motion-in-limine deadline does not apply), and missing it waives Daubert arguments. Choice-of-law motions are due by the dispositive motion deadline, and the court may defer ruling without a full factual record. A motion to extend time under Rules 6(b), 31, 33, 34, or 36 must state the original due date, the number of prior extensions and when the last expires, the reason the action is not done, and whether opposing counsel agrees (agreement does not bind the court).

docs.x: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr., W.D. Mo.. Exhibits (trap): Designate exhibits P1, D1, or J1, give the courtroom deputy an exhibit index on the clerk’s form, and list page or part counts for multi-page exhibits. Impeachment-only exhibits need not be listed. Mark exhibits individually: a page or portion to be admitted alone needs its own number, and partial admission or “sub-exhibit” numbers are not allowed. Check the list for numbering errors before trial. Confer to agree on admissible exhibits and jointly pre-admit them with a list of those in dispute, and agree in advance on any exhibits to be used in opening statements.

docs.t: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. (W.D. Mo.) — Civil trial filings
docs.x: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr., W.D. Mo.. Civil trial filings: Jury instructions are due 21 days before trial, filed jointly and annotated, drawn from the Eighth Circuit model civil instructions and/or MAI, with modifications disclosed and each labeled only “Instruction No. ___.” Disputed instructions need a written objection with authority and an alternative, due 14 days before trial. Email clean and annotated Word versions to the courtroom deputy. Proposed voir dire is due 14 days before trial, and a trial brief of no more than two or three pages summarizing the evidence by witness and exhibit (not reciting pleadings or elements) 7 days before trial. Four days before trial, file a list of everyone who will sit at counsel table; each must be present during voir dire, or may not come before the rail during trial. Trial starts at 8:00 a.m.

docs.t: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr. (W.D. Mo.) — Trial conduct (trap)

If the parties agree, the jury is instructed before openings and again before closings, and jurors may submit written questions to witnesses, with objections taken at sidebar. The court asks all voir dire questions unless counsel ask at the pretrial hearing for extensive participation. To object, stand and say “Your honor, objection,” then give a brief basis; no speeches, and sidebars are very limited. Raise legal issues by written motion before trial; testimony will not be interrupted for evident

docs.x: Judge Willie J. Epps, Jr., W.D. Mo.. Settlement and contact: Notify the courtroom deputy by email within 10 days after settlement negotiations take place. docs.t: Judge D. Edward Snow (E.D. Okla.) — Exhibit notebooks (trap)
docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. Exhibit notebooks (trap): Prepare separate exhibit notebooks for the witness stand, opposing counsel, the court, and the court’s law clerk. The court’s and law clerk’s notebooks are due at least one week before the pretrial conference and at least three days before any motion hearing. With voluminous exhibits, prepare a notebook for each witness (or group testifying together) and have it on the stand before questioning, to avoid trips to the witness.

docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. Give the court as much advance notice as possible of any particularly difficult legal or evidentiary question, and provide objections to proposed jury instructions, with case law, before trial.

docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. Voir dire and openings: The court conducts most of voir dire; limited questioning by counsel is generally allowed. Counsel may not preview evidence or law, ask disguised statements or hypotheticals, explain the burden of proof, or seek promises or verdict commitments from jurors. The court limits opening statements; request the time you need. Openings outline the evidence and may not argue.

Stand and use the lectern to address the court or question witnesses. docs.t: Judge D. Edward Snow (E.D. Okla.) — Courtroom conduct (trap)
docs.x: Judge D. Edward Snow, E.D. Okla.. Courtroom conduct (trap): Follow Local Rule 83.7(b) on courtroom behavior. Do not leave the courtroom during trial or address opposing counsel directly in open court without leave; never interrupt the court. Computer use must be unobtrusive and cleared with the courtroom deputy before the morning of trial. No gum, mints, candy, or beverages (including bottled water); keep items that could scratch off the courtroom furniture. Address the jury from the lectern at a respectful distance. Keep objections short, do not argue them or the ruling, or make motions such as for mistrial, in front of the jury, and keep bench conferences to a minimum. The court will not declare a witness qualified as an expert in the jury’s presence, and counsel should not ask it to.

Sealed documents may be unsealed at the court’s discretion. To challenge a designation, confer first, then give notice and move for a ruling; the designating party bears the burden, and the material stays confidential until the court rules.

Within sixty business days after final resolution, confidential material must be returned or destroyed; counsel may keep marked work product, filings, transcripts, and the trial record.

docs.t: Judge Jason A. Robertson (E.D. Okla.) — Candor and AI in filings (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jason A. Robertson, E.D. Okla.. Candor and AI in filings (trap): The court does not restrict or require disclosure of drafting or research tools, including technology, but the signer is fully responsible for every filing. A reasonable inquiry requires human verification of cited authority; relying on automated output alone is not enough. Any citation to nonexistent authority (hallucinated cases, fabricated quotations, invented statutes, or materially inaccurate descriptions) may be a violation, even if isolated. Disclosing use of a tool is no safe harbor. Pro se litigants are held to the same duties under the standards for unrepresented parties. Sanctions are proportionate and may include striking the filing, an order to show cause, monetary sanctions, or referral to disciplinary authorities. Contact: chambers 918-684-7960; courtroom deputy Joe Church.

docs.t: Judge Raymond E. Patricco (D. Idaho) — Scheduling conference

Scheduling conference: Each party files a litigation plan and a discovery plan one week before the scheduling conference, or the parties may stipulate and file one litigation plan and a joint discovery plan (encouraged). docs.t: Judge Raymond E. Patricco (D. Idaho) — ADR
docs.x: Judge Raymond E. Patricco, D. Idaho. ADR: Discuss ADR with your client before the Rule 16 scheduling conference and report there on the client’s willingness to participate and preferred form (mediation, judicially assisted settlement conference, or arbitration). A mediator is chosen by mutual agreement, and the mediator submits a Mediation Status Report to the court’s ADR Coordinator within 10 days after the process ends. Arbitration referral only by stipulation. A magistrate-judge settlement conference may be requested at any time with enough time before trial; when all parties agree, it is set on a mutually agreeable date and a settlement conference order issues.

docs.x: Judge Raymond E. Patricco, D. Idaho. Contact and status inquiries: Courtroom deputy Brandi Fifer, (208) 334-9023, handles scheduling and changes to hearing dates or times. docs.t: Judge Stephen R. Welby (E.D. Mo.) — Treating providers as experts
docs.x: Judge Stephen R. Welby, E.D. Mo.. Treating providers as experts: Treating providers testifying to matters in their treatment notes need not prepare Rule 26(a)(2)(B) reports but are normally limited to opinions related to the treatment and disclosed in the notes; reports may be required, for example, on causation.

docs.t: Judge Stephen R. Welby (E.D. Mo.) — ADR
docs.x: Judge Stephen R. Welby, E.D. Mo.. ADR: Most civil cases are referred to ADR; discuss mediation timing at the Rule 16 conference. ADR deadlines are binding and extended only by court order.

docs.t: Judge Stephen R. Welby (E.D. Mo.) — Pretrial deadlines (trap)
docs.x: Judge Stephen R. Welby, E.D. Mo.. Pretrial deadlines (trap): If the case is still pending two weeks before trial, chambers will contact you to schedule a final pretrial conference, usually the week before trial; be ready to argue motions in limine. Joint proposed jury instructions are due no later than 10 days before the final pretrial conference and objections no later than 5 days before it. Use Eighth Circuit Model instructions when possible; others need case authority. If the court conducts all of voir dire, submit proposed questions no later than two business days before trial.

docs.t: Judge Stephen R. Welby (E.D. Mo.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Stephen R. Welby, E.D. Mo.. Trial: Attorneys conduct most of voir dire after the court’s introduction, without rapport-building, promises, speeches, or argument. Challenges for cause are made outside the panel’s presence. Exhibits may be used in opening with opposing counsel’s consent and advance notice. State objections in a word or phrase, with no argument before the jury; recross only if redirect raises something new. Stand when the jury enters and when speaking; no food, drink other than water, gum, or social media. Attorneys may use phones in the courtroom only without disrupting the court. Follow Local Rule 13.05 for sealed documents.

docs.t: Judge Anne Y. Shields (E.D.N.Y.) — Contacting chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Anne Y. Shields, E.D.N.Y.. Calls on the substance of a matter must be joint, with opposing counsel on the line. Emailing chambers is prohibited without prior authorization. Confer and file a joint communication on ECF; if that is impracticable, file a letter on ECF. Any request for relief must be filed on ECF as a “Motion,” not as a “Letter” under “Other Documents.”

docs.t: Judge Anne Y. Shields (E.D.N.Y.) — Courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Anne Y. Shields, E.D.N.Y.. Courtesy copies: Courtesy copies are required only for motions with all exhibits and for motions referred by a District Judge. Mark them “Courtesy Copy” and “Original Filed ECF” with the docket number, tab and label exhibits (binders where appropriate, no Velobinding), and mail them to chambers on the filing date. The movant furnishes a full courtesy set of the fully briefed motion with a cover letter listing each document, copied to opposing counsel.

Judge Shields cannot extend deadlines, including discovery deadlines, set by the District Judge; ask the District Judge.

Memoranda: 25 pages for opening and opposition, 10 for reply, no further br

docs.t: Judge Anne Y. Shields (E.D.N.Y.) — Settlement conferences (trap)
docs.x: Judge Anne Y. Shields, E.D.N.Y.. Parties may instead request referral to the EDNY Mediation Program.

Jury trials: 2 weeks before jury selection, file a statement of anticipated in limine issues (a pre-motion conference follows), evidentiary stipulations, and proposed charges on the elements only. Bring labeled, indexed, tabbed exhibit binders on day one. Bench trials: trial memorandum 1 week before trial; proposed findings and conclusions, with transcript and exhibit citations, 2 weeks after the transcript is available.

docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. AI disclosure (trap): Any attorney or pro se party who used AI to prepare a filed document must disclose that use and certify in the document that the accuracy of any generative-AI-drafted portion, including all citations and authority, has been checked.

docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. Summary judgment in consent cases (trap): Before any pre-motion request, the movant serves a Local Rule 56.1 statement with citations to admissible evidence; opponents serve an original and two copies of a counter-statement within 7 business days. No conference is held until the parties comply with Rule 56.1; the briefing schedule is set at the conference.

docs.t: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay (E.D.N.Y.) — Pro hac vice
docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. Pro hac vice: Serve and file the motion with a proposed order at least 7 business days before the return date; no memorandum needed, and it is decided on submission. Opposition is due at least 2 business days before the return date; no replies.

docs.t: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay (E.D.N.Y.) — Social Security appeals
docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. Social Security appeals: Cases filed on or after December 1, 2022 follow Administrative Order 2023-06. Mail one hard courtesy copy of the motion papers and stipulation; defendant mails one copy of the record; in counseled cases, email a Word version of the stipulation to chambers. In counseled cases, the parties prepare a two-part stipulation of facts with a medical chronology: undisputed facts in chronological order with record citations, and disputed facts with concise statements. Plaintiff must state each alleged legal error or unsupported ALJ finding with record citations, and defendant must respond to each. Omissions may lead to denial, waiver, or striking of the opposition.

docs.t: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay (E.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial in consent cases
docs.x: Judge Arlene R. Lindsay, E.D.N.Y.. Late or incomplete submissions may lead to rescheduling the trial. 15 days before trial, file requests to charge (elements, damages, and defenses only) and voir dire in jury cases, a proposed verdict sheet by claim, an elements-and-facts statement in bench cases, motions in limine, and any optional pretrial memorandum.

docs.x: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky, E.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): Requests for adjournments, extensions, or conference changes (including to appear by phone) must be letter motions filed as a “Motion,” not a “Letter” or “Status Report,” at least 3 business days before the date, absent emergency. State the original date, number of prior requests, effect on other dates, the reason, and each party’s position. Extending discovery or case-management deadlines needs Rule 16(b)(4) good cause even on consent, and another party’s noncompliance is no basis unless the movant timely pursued remedies.

docs.t: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky (E.D.N.Y.) — Initial conference
docs.x: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky, E.D.N.Y.. Initial conference: Initial conferences are usually in person; the plaintiff or removing defendant must notify all parties of the date. The form covers jurisdiction (each LLC member’s citizenship in diversity cases), damages computations, settlement, ESI, a confidentiality or Rule 502(d) order, the schedule (later written discovery served at least 30 days before the fact cutoff), experts, and consent or Direct Assignment acknowledgment.

docs.t: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes (trap): Raise disputes under Local Civil Rule 37.2, modified: one jointly composed letter motion of no more than 5 pages, filed as a “Motion”; write separately only if the other side won’t cooperate. Describe meet-and-confer efforts (time, place, duration, counsel), state each issue and the relief sought, cite authority, and excerpt only the disputed requests. No bulk objections. Delay in seeking help can waive the discovery, especially near the close of discovery. Deposition disputes: email and call chambers immediately with a callback number, keep the deposition going (have the reporter mark the spot), and have the reporter on the call when the court returns it.

The form limits confidential designations to listed categories (sensitive commercial or personal data, medical and legal records, non-public criminal history), allows deposition designation within 10 days of receiving the transcript, and requires following the EDNY sealed-filing steps.

In consent cases with all parties represented (except habeas and Social Security), Rule 12 and Rule 56 motions need a pre-motion letter motion of no more than 3 pages; responses of no more than 3 pages are due within 1 week, with no replies. A timely letter counts as timely service of the motion, and the court may treat the letter as the motion. FRAP 4(a)(4) motions and motions whose delay would cost a substantive right are exempt.

An unexcused absence can mean reimbursing others’ time and travel. Plaintiff conveys a proposal at least 14 days before, and defendant at least 8 days before; each must include a rationale, not a bare number. One week before, each represented party emails a confidential ex parte statement of no more than 5 pages covering the issues, authorities and comparators, negotiation history, counsel’s valuation and rationale, strengths and weaknesses, other helpful information, and who will attend. Key exhibits are optional; media files go through the court’s evidence portal. The c

docs.t: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky (E.D.N.Y.) — Trials on consent
docs.x: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky, E.D.N.Y.. Trials on consent: The joint proposed pretrial order is due 60 days after the close of all discovery or 30 days after any summary judgment ruling, whichever is later, including damages calculations, witnesses with summaries, deposition designations, and an exhibit table (pre-marked PX, DX, and JX) with objections and responses. The court then sets a firm trial date. Daubert motions are due no later than the pretrial order; other motions in limine at least 3 weeks before trial, in a single submission per party, with responses 1 week later. Jury trials: joint requests to charge, verdict sheet, and case-specific voir dire (with a brief case statement and list of names) due 2 weeks before trial, also emailed to chambers in word-processing format. Bench trials: pretrial memoranda 2 weeks before. Two tabbed exhibit binders are due by the Thursday before trial.

docs.t: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky (E.D.N.Y.) — Pro se cases
docs.x: Judge Clay H. Kaminsky, E.D.N.Y.. Pro se cases: Pro se litigants are exempt from ECF but may request electronic filing. Counsel must serve ECF filings on pro se parties not receiving electronic notice, file certificates of service, and review Local Civil Rules 7.2, 12.1, 33.2, and 56.2.

docs.x: Judge James M. Wicks, E.D.N.Y.. docs.x: Judge James M. Wicks, E.D.N.Y.. docs.x: Judge James M. Wicks, E.D.N.Y.. docs.x: Judge James R. Cho, E.D.N.Y.. Other non-dispositive motions: After good-faith efforts, proceed by letter motion under Local Civil Rule 7.1(e), using judgment on length; the court may direct a formal motion under Local Civil Rules 6.1 and 7.1.

In consent cases, Rule 12 and 56 motions need a pre-motion conference letter of no more than 1,050 words with an agreed briefing schedule after conferring; a timely letter counts as timely service of the motion. Responses (1,050 words max) are due within 7 days. The court may treat the letter and conference argument as the motion. No fixed page limits, but memoranda of 10 pages or more need a table of contents; 1-inch margins, double spacing, 12-point text (10-point footnotes). No legal argument in affidavits or declarations. docs.x: Judge James R. Cho, E.D.N.Y.. Settlement conferences: A party representative (other than outside counsel) familiar with the matter and with full authority must attend, with the responsible attorney. At least 7 days before, email cho_chambers@nyed.uscourts.gov an ex parte letter of no more than 1,750 words (about 5 pages, excluding exhibits) covering the status of talks, the last demand and offer, strengths and weaknesses, and other helpful information.

docs.x: Judge James R. Cho, E.D.N.Y.. Confidentiality orders: A form confidentiality order is posted; to change it, submit a redline with reasons and a clean version. docs.t: Judge James R. Cho (E.D.N.Y.) — Trials
docs.x: Judge James R. Cho, E.D.N.Y.. Trials: In cases for the District Judge, file the joint pretrial order in that judge’s format. In consent cases, the joint pretrial order must include witnesses (including impeachment and rebuttal) with testimony summaries, deposition designations, and an exhibit schedule (including anticipated impeachment exhibits) with objections; exhibits are pre-marked, exchanged, and delivered to the court 2 weeks before trial. 4 weeks before a consent trial, file motions in limine (responses 3 weeks before, replies 2 weeks before), any bench-trial memorandum, requests to charge on elements, damages, and defenses, and joint voir dire and verdict form. The court generally does not provide civil interpreters; a friend or relative may interpret but must translate exactly.

docs.t: Judge Lee G. Dunst (E.D.N.Y.) — Appearances
docs.x: Judge Lee G. Dunst, E.D.N.Y.. Appearances: Appearances are generally in person, though some are by video or phone as the scheduling order or docket calendar says. Counsel must be prepared and authorized to discuss progress, scheduling, and settlement, and must file a notice of appearance first. “Of counsel” attorneys may not appear without the represented party’s explicit authorization; any lawyer employed by the firm of record may appear. Junior lawyers are strongly encouraged to argue and examine witnesses, and saying a junior lawyer will argue may tip the court toward holding argument. No court interpreters in civil cases: represented non-English-speaking parties ordered to appear must bring a professional interpreter.

docs.x: Judge Lee G. Dunst, E.D.N.Y.. Counsel who know the case must attend. No automatic stay of discovery; start discovery before the initial conference. Phase One (initial disclosures and readily available documents) is presumptively complete within 60 days of the conference, followed by settlement efforts; Phase Two proceeds only if settlement fails. Amendment or joinder after the court-set deadline requires Rule 16(b)(4) good cause.

Conferences and initial scheduling: File a notice of appearance before appearing; only counsel of record or an attorney personally authorized by the party may appear. Law students and junior attorneys are encouraged to argue under supervision, and multiple lawyers may argue for a party. Initial conferences are typically in person absent a compelling reason. After the Rule 26(f) meeting, file the joint proposed Discovery Plan and Scheduling Order at least 1 week before the conference, noting disagreements in a joint letter. The form presumes initial disclosures and first discovery requests by the initial conference, a joint status report 45 days after it, fact discovery within 90–150 days, and all discovery within 9 months; Direct Assignment cases file a consent or acknowledgment form within 7 days of the conference. Once so ordered, deadlines chang

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes (trap): After a good-faith effort under Rule 37(a)(1), file a single joint letter as a “Motion” for an informal discovery conference (Local Civil Rule 37.2), starting with a brief statement of the claims and defenses and describing the conferral; each side’s portion is limited to 2 pages, with the disputed requests attached. If not resolved informally, the court may order formal briefing; cost-shifting is presumptively mandatory under Rule 37(a)(5). Deposition disputes: email and call chambers immediately with a brief description and callback number, have the reporter mark the transcript, continue on other issues, and have the reporter on the call when the court calls back.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Motions (trap): Non-dispositive motions (e.g., to amend, stay discovery, or conditionally certify a collective) go to Judge Cross-Goldenberg unless the District Judge directs otherwise, generally as letter motions under Local Civil Rule 7.1(e); the court may direct a formal motion. Dispositive motions go to the District Judge unless the parties consent. In consent cases, no pre-motion conference is needed and there is no bundling rule; file under the Federal and Local Rules, with memoranda conforming to Local Rule 7.1.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Settlement conferences: Each party, or a non-lawyer with settlement authority, must attend unless permission to participate by phone was granted in advance. Exchange a good-faith demand and offer at least 2 weeks before the conference and before submitting statements. Email confidential ex parte statements at least 1 week before, with the last demand and offer, a realistic assessment, client priorities, and barriers to settlement; a few key exhibits are optional (media via the court’s evidence portal). The court may contact counsel individually beforehand.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Confidentiality orders
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Confidentiality orders: A form Confidentiality Order is posted; to change it, submit a redline with reasons and a clean version. It limits confidential designations to listed categories, allows deposition designation within 10 days of receiving the transcript, and requires following the EDNY sealed-filing steps.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial and trial
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Pretrial and trial: File the joint proposed pretrial order in the District Judge’s format by the deadline. In consent cases, the court sets a firm trial date after discovery closes and issues pretrial order instructions then.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg (E.D.N.Y.) — Pro se cases
docs.x: Judge Peggy Cross-Goldenberg, E.D.N.Y.. Pro se cases: Pro se litigants are exempt from ECF but may request electronic filing; their filings are docketed on receipt, which serves ECF users. Counsel must send pro se parties copies of ECF filings and file proof of service.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Communicating with chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Communicating with chambers (trap): All communications go through ECF. Phone calls only when immediate attention is required (for example, to alert the court to an emergency filing); faxes only with permission; email only for confidential settlement statements or as directed. Call the ECF Help Desk (718-613-2312), not chambers, with ECF problems. Documents filed on a non-business day are deemed filed the next business day. No courtesy copies unless asked; don’t send or file correspondence between counsel or discovery materials unless needed for a request for judicial intervention.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): Requests to adjourn or change a conference (including to appear by phone) and to extend court deadlines must be letters filed as a “Motion,” not a “Letter,” at least 2 business days before, absent emergency. Never request an adjournment by phone (though you may call to flag a last-minute emergency request after filing it). State the original date or deadline, the reason, the number of prior requests, and whether others consent (with their reasons, or efforts to reach them). If other dates are affected, attach a revised Proposed Discovery Plan/Scheduling Order, and for extensions also ask to adjourn affected conferences.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Initial conference
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Initial conference: At least 10 business days before the initial conference, meet and confer, exchange initial disclosures, and complete the judge’s Proposed Discovery Plan/Scheduling Order; file it at least 5 business days before. Be ready to give an overview of the facts and issues and outline discovery; counsel who know the case must attend with authority to commit to a schedule and discuss mediation or settlement.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — FLSA cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. FLSA cases (trap): The posted FLSA order waives Rule 26(a)(1) disclosures and stays other discovery. Within the set period (45 days on the form), plaintiff serves wage documents, a written account of the claim, any collective description, and fees to date; defendant serves time and payroll records, pay policies, proof on disputed individual liability, and any financial records it relies on for settlement. Counsel then meet in person to try to settle (with clients with authority available by phone) and file a joint status report within 7 days; if unsettled, mediate under Local Civil Rule 83.8 within the set period and report within 7 days afterward, then request a settlement conference or file a Proposed Discovery Plan. Strict adherence is expected and noncompliance is sanctionable; changes need good cause and a joint ECF letter.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes: Confer in person or by phone first (Local Civil Rule 37.3(a)). Then file a joint letter of no more than 3 pages as a “Motion,” attaching the disputed requests; the court usually holds a phone conference and may order a motion to compel. Don’t file discovery material unless needed.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Non-dispositive motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Non-dispositive motions (trap): At least 2 days before filing a non-discovery motion, tell the other parties and give them a chance to consent; file the motion with a letter certifying compliance and stating their position (or efforts to reach them). No pre-motion conference needed. Oppositions are due within 10 business days and replies within 5 business days. Memoranda are limited to 12 double-spaced pages, replies to 5, unless permitted.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Dispositive motions in consent cases
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Dispositive motions in consent cases: Dispositive motions go to the District Judge unless all parties consent in writing (for the whole case or one motion). In consent cases, file a motion for a pre-motion conference with a summary of no more than 3 pages; responses of 3 pages are due within 5 business days; no replies. The briefing schedule is set at the conference. Memoranda: 25 double-spaced pages, replies 10, unless modified. Request oral argument by letter with the papers; more than one lawyer may argue per side.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Settlement conferences: Each party or a non-lawyer with settlement authority must attend unless phone participation was approved in advance. Exchange a demand and offer beforehand. Email confidential ex parte statements to kuo_chambers@nyed.uscourts.gov at least 7 business days before, with the last demand and offer, a realistic assessment, client priorities, and barriers to settlement.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Confidentiality and sealing
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Confidentiality and sealing: Any confidentiality order must follow the judge’s form; propose changes in track changes or similar. Motions to seal are filed on ECF with the proposed sealed documents attached, under the EDNY instructions.

docs.t: Judge Peggy Kuo (E.D.N.Y.) — Trials on consent
docs.x: Judge Peggy Kuo, E.D.N.Y.. Trials on consent: Proposed joint pretrial order due within 60 days after discovery closes, including elements of claims and defenses, damages, witnesses (including rebuttal) with summaries, designations, an exhibit schedule (P- and D-prefixed, including impeachment and rebuttal exhibits) with objections, and a list of proposed motions in limine. Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged at least 10 business days before trial; the court needs four copies. Requests to charge and voir dire (jury) or an elements-and-facts statement (bench) are due 1 week before trial. Relatively inexperienced attorneys are strongly encouraged to participate, with supervision in complex hearings, and should get a full opportunity to argue.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Filing and communications
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Filing and communications: All documents directed to Judge Levy must be e-filed, whatever District Judge is assigned. A lawyer seeking an ECF exemption must apply within 2 weeks of the Initial Conference Order, stating specific good-cause hardship; granted only in limited circumstances. Except for pro se parties, all communications with chambers are filed on ECF; don’t send hard copies of filings or correspondence between counsel without authorization, and include the case name, docket number, and judges’ initials. Phone calls are permitted; scheduling and calendar matters go to Janine Marino (718-613-2340). No faxes without authorization.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): Make requests by letter filed under “Motions,” not as a “Letter” under “Other Documents,” stating the original date, the reason, how much more time is needed, the number of prior requests and whether granted, and the adversary’s position and reasons. Include a proposed revised scheduling order if other dates are affected. Requests to adjourn a court appearance are due at least 2 business days before, absent emergency; don’t call to request an adjournment except in an emergency.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes: Non-dispositive pretrial motions go to Judge Levy; dispositive motions (including venue) go to the District Judge. After a good-faith effort under Rule 37(a)(1) and Local Civil Rule 37.3(a), describe the dispute in a single jointly composed letter, with each side’s portion limited to 3 pages, describing the conferral efforts.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Consent cases and dispositive motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Consent cases and dispositive motions (trap): Parties may consent for all purposes or only for a dispositive motion or approval of a settlement or infant compromise. In consent cases, a pre-motion conference (by phone with permission) is required before any dispositive motion, except where the movant is pro se or in habeas, prisoner, Social Security, or bankruptcy appeal cases. Request it by letter of no more than 3 pages; responses of no more than 3 pages are due within 7 days of service. A movant’s letter served within Rule 12 time counts as timely service of a Rule 12(b) motion. No fixed page limits (the court may impose them). File motion papers promptly after service, submit marked courtesy copies of all motion papers, and request oral argument by letter when filing.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Pretrial in consent cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Pretrial in consent cases (trap): Joint pretrial order due within 60 days after the discovery completion date, including witnesses (live or by deposition), designations, and an exhibit schedule (including impeachment and rebuttal exhibits) with objections. Failing to object in the pretrial order waives all objections at trial except relevance, and meritless authenticity or chain-of-custody objections may draw sanctions. Exhibits are pre-marked and exchanged at least 10 days before trial. 15 days before trial (or 30 days after the final pretrial order if no trial date is set), file requests to charge and voir dire, a detailed damages statement by claim, an elements-and-facts statement in bench cases, motions in limine, and any optional pretrial memorandum.

docs.t: Judge Robert M. Levy (E.D.N.Y.) — Confidentiality orders and sealing
docs.x: Judge Robert M. Levy, E.D.N.Y.. Confidentiality orders and sealing: The judge’s Confidentiality Standing Order limits confidential designations to listed categories, allows deposition designation within 10 days of receiving the transcript, and requires experts and witnesses to sign Exhibit A before seeing confidential documents. Under the order, filings that reveal confidential material are filed under seal only as to the specific designated documents and the portions of briefs containing that material, absent independent good cause.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Communicating with chambers (trap)
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Communicating with chambers (trap): Use ECF with the right event type (a letter asking for action is usually a “motion,” not a “letter” or “status report”) and a brief description. No courtesy copies unless directed. Phone calls only as the rules allow, as instructed, or for emergencies; scheduling questions may go to the courtroom deputy (718-510-9714). Email only as the rules allow, copying all counsel unless it is an authorized ex parte submission; urgent issues go by phone, not email. Notify chambers immediately by phone or email of possible recusal grounds, or of a settlement if you can’t promptly file on ECF.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Adjournments and extensions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Adjournments and extensions (trap): File as a “Motion” (not a “Letter”) at least 2 business days before the appearance or deadline; a late request needs a good-faith basis and a phone call to chambers. State the date, prior requests by any party and their outcome, others’ positions and reasons, and effects on other dates; propose a revised schedule, or at least three new conference dates when all parties are available. A request to convert an in-person conference to phone or video counts as an adjournment request and needs good cause. Filing a request does not stay any deadline or conference; comply unless it is granted, and call chambers if a deadline is near.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Appearances and initial conference
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Appearances and initial conference: File a notice of appearance before appearing. Counsel must be fully familiar with the case, the orders, and the rules, and authorized to discuss progress, scheduling, and settlement, or the party may be treated as failing to appear. Junior attorneys and supervised law students are encouraged to participate. Hold the Rule 26(f) conference at least 1 week before the initial conference and file the joint proposed discovery plan on the court’s model at least 7 days before. Exchange initial disclosures beforehand, and ideally first interrogatories, document requests, and releases, or be ready to explain why not. The model presumes fact discovery within 90–150 days and all discovery within 240 days of the initial conference.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery disputes (trap)
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery disputes (trap): Don’t file discovery requests or responses. After good-faith efforts under Rule 37(a)(1) and Local Civil Rules 26.4 and 37.2, file one jointly composed letter as a “motion” seeking a discovery conference (also file as a “motion” any status report raising a dispute), covering the dispute, each side’s position on facts and law, and conferral efforts; each side’s portion is limited to 3 pages. Attach only the relevant requests and responses. Absent unforeseen circumstances, motions to compel made later than 30 days before the close of discovery are untimely. Deposition disputes: call chambers with all parties on the line; continue the deposition where possible while waiting, and never stop it without contacting the court.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Confidentiality orders
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Confidentiality orders: If the parties agree to the form order, file it signed as a “consent motion” with a cover letter describing the information covered. To change it, submit a letter explaining the changes and each side’s position, a redline, and a clean version, and email the proposed order to chambers in Word.

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Settlement (trap)
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Settlement (trap): Be prepared to discuss settlement at every appearance; demands and offers are encouraged as early as the Rule 26(f) conference. Attorneys at a settlement conference must be authorized to settle on the record, and clients are expected to attend in person unless the court says otherwise. Plaintiff serves a demand with a brief explanation at least 14 days before; defendant serves an offer with an explanation at least 7 days before; co-defendants with different counsel exchange letters on contribution. At least 5 business days before, email ex parte letters (5 pages max, excluding attachments) covering demands and offers, strengths and weaknesses, valuation with authorities and comparable verdicts and settlements, obstacles, and any special terms sought (confidentiality, indemnification, etc.). docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Motions (trap): Non-dispositive motions go to Judge Eichenholtz unless the District Judge directs otherwise: discovery motions under Section VI and Local Civil Rule 37.2; others by letter motion under Local Civil Rule 7.1(e) after good-faith efforts, or by requesting a conference. In consent cases, except Social Security and habeas, request a pre-motion conference before any Rule 12 or 56 motion, venue motion, or Rule 15 motion needing leave: a letter of no more than 3 pages with citations (for summary judgment, describing the key undisputed facts; for amendment, complying with Local Civil Rule 15.1). A pre-motion letter seeking to move to dismiss stays the time to answer through the conference. Responses (3 pages max) are due within 5 business days and must say whether the plaintiff will amend as of right, seek leave, or brief the motion; summary jud

docs.t: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz (E.D.N.Y.) — Trials on consent
docs.x: Judge Seth D. Eichenholtz, E.D.N.Y.. Trials on consent: Joint proposed pretrial order due within 60 days after the discovery completion date, including witnesses with summaries, designations, and an exhibit table (exhibit, description, objections, response), with exhibits pre-marked in order of use (numbers for plaintiff, letters for defendant). Motions in limine at least 15 days before trial, attaching disputed documents; responses 5 days later. Jury instructions, voir dire, and verdict sheet at least 10 days before trial, also emailed in Word; bench-trial memoranda, if requested, 10 days before. Each party brings three tabbed exhibit binders to the final pretrial conference, after exchanging all exhibits.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Conferences in person (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Conferences in person (trap): All conferences are in person in Room 820, Central Islip; responsible counsel must attend, and phone appearances are not allowed absent exceptional circumstances. If you will be late, tell your adversary (or, if unavailable, the court) and give an arrival time. The judge usually sets a status conference after the first round of document discovery; if nothing needs attention, file a joint status letter as a “Motion” asking to cancel it.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Filing, courtesy copies, and sealing
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Filing, courtesy copies, and sealing: Any letter requesting court intervention (including Local Civil Rule 37.1 and 37.3 letters and discovery-deadline extensions) must be docketed under “Motions,” not as a “Letter” under “Other Documents.” Send hard copies only of letter motions whose exhibits or attachments exceed 15 pages in total, and of referred motions or motions on notice to Judge Locke, marked “Courtesy Copy” with the ECF docket number and with protruding tabbed exhibit dividers. No courtesy copies of dispositive motions before the District Judge unless referred. Nothing may be filed under seal without prior permission.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Communications and adjournments (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Communications and adjournments (trap): Phone calls are permitted: criminal questions to Kristin Gandiosi (631-712-5724), others to 631-712-5720. Calls seeking relief need all parties on the line, and calls from a deposition need the court reporter present. Adjournment and extension requests must be filed as motions at least 2 business days before the appearance, absent emergency, stating the original date, the reason, whether all parties consent (and why not), and the number of prior requests. Adjournment requests must list at least three alternative dates when all parties are available; extension requests must show good cause and include a proposed amended scheduling order where appropriate. No courtesy copies.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Discovery and non-dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Discovery and non-dispositive motions: Letter motions under Local Civil Rules 37.1 and 37.3, filed as a “Motion,” after a good-faith effort to resolve the dispute in person or by phone: 3 pages max excluding attachments, responses of 3 pages within 4 days, no replies. Letters use 1-inch margins, single spacing, and 12-point font. No pre-motion conference. Such motions may instead be made on notice under Local Civil Rule 6.1, following the motion-on-notice rules.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Motions on notice (trap)
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Motions on notice (trap): Bundle rule: no papers are filed until fully briefed and exchanged, and the movant files all papers on the same date. Exempt: pro hac vice motions, Local Civil Rule 6.3 reconsideration of Judge Locke’s orders, and in consent cases Rule 50, 52, 59, or 60 motions, FRAP 4(a)(5) motions, and orders to show cause. Compliance with these rules does not excuse missing FRAP 4 deadlines. Memoranda: 25 pages for opening and opposition, 10 for reply; table of contents at 10 pages or more; pinpoint cites; 1-inch margins, double spacing, 12-point font. Legal argument in affidavits is rejected, as are noncompliant papers. Oral argument may be requested.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Summary judgment in consent cases
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Summary judgment in consent cases: Dispositive motions go to the District Judge unless the parties consent. In consent cases with all parties represented, file a letter stating the basis for the motion and an agreed briefing schedule; no pre-motion conference is needed, and the court approves or sets the schedule. The movant serves a Local Civil Rule 56.1 statement, notice of motion, memorandum, and supporting papers; the opponent serves a counterstatement with paragraphs matching the movant’s, a memorandum, and support; then the reply. Against a pro se party, also serve and include a Local Civil Rule 56.2 notice. Noncompliant papers are rejected.

docs.t: Judge Steven I. Locke (E.D.N.Y.) — Social Security appeals on consent
docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Social Security appeals on consent: Defendant serves (not files) the record within 60 days of the scheduling order, and the answer is waived. Plaintiff serves its motion for judgment on the pleadings within 45 days of the record, defendant its cross-motion within 45 days after that, and any reply within 30 days; the movant then files everything with the record under the bundle rule, with hard courtesy copies of the papers and the record. Counseled plaintiffs must include a numbered “Statement of Contentions” identifying each legal error or unsupported ALJ finding with pinpoint record cites; defendant responds paragraph by paragraph in an “Opposing Statement of Contentions.” Omissions can mean denial, waiver, or a stricken opposition.

docs.x: Judge Steven I. Locke, E.D.N.Y.. Settlement conferences (trap): Request one by joint letter with three dates when all attorneys and parties are available. All attorneys and parties must appear in person, and entities must send someone with authority. The parties must complete one round of demand and response beforehand. Three days before, email an ex parte letter to the courtroom deputy (kristin_gandiosi@nyed.uscourts.gov), not on ECF, covering the facts, relevant case law, negotiation history, and a realistic assessment.

At least 2 weeks before trial, file fully briefed motions in limine, requests to charge (also emailed in Word to the courtroom deputy) and voir dire, a damages statement by claim (jury), an elements-and-facts statement (bench), any optional memorandum, and one set of pre-marked exhibit binders.

docs.x: Judge Steven L. Tiscione, E.D.N.Y.. docs.x: Judge Steven L. Tiscione, E.D.N.Y.. Merely copying the adversary is not enough. Requests lacking any of these are denied: the original date, the number of prior requests and their outcome, the adversary’s position and reasons, the reason for the request, and a suggested new date or revised schedule with specific dates.

docs.t: Judge Steven L. Tiscione (E.D.N.Y.) — Initial conference and phased discovery
docs.x: Judge Steven L. Tiscione, E.D.N.Y.. Initial conference and phased discovery: In cases where all parties have counsel, complete the Discovery Plan Worksheet attached to the Initial Conference Order and file it at least 2 days before the initial conference; in pro se cases the court completes it with the parties at the conference. Entered deadlines change only for good cause. Phase I covers what is needed for reasoned settlement talks, presumptively within 60 days, with each party itemizing it on the worksheet; an initial settlement conference follows about 10–15 days later. Phase II (the rest of discovery) proceeds only if settlement fails. The worksheet presumes all discovery ends 9 months after the initial conference. Be prepared and authorized to discuss settlement at every appearance.

docs.t: Judge Suzanne Mitchell (W.D. Okla.) — Protective orders and sealing (trap)
docs.x: Judge Suzanne Mitchell, W.D. Okla.. Protective orders and sealing (trap): Judge Mitchell will not sign a protective order that lets counsel decide what is confidential. The proposed order must list the categories covered (for example, personnel files, medical information, confidential financial matters), and the motion must explain why each category needs confidentiality. The judge will not sign an order letting confidential-designated items be filed under seal for that reason. The order must require a motion, filed and noticed for hearing before the filing’s due date, showing good cause to seal; a confidentiality designation alone is not enough. A protective order is not a binding good-cause finding if a party later seeks relief from it; the court will balance privacy and public access anew.
